newsitem.title: GERMANY: Officials say BSE calf was probably German-born.
newsitem.headline: Officials say BSE calf was probably German-born.

text.p: A Galloway calf at the centre of a mad cow disease scare was apparently born in Germany and was unlikely to have been illegally imported from Britain, officials said on Friday.

The calf was believed to be the first German-born cow to contract Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), known as mad cow disease, prompting the Agriculture Ministry to announce the slaughter of 5,100 cattle imported from Britain and Switzerland.
The Agriculture Ministry said earlier it was investigating the possibility that the calf first thought to have been born in Germany had been imported illegally from Britain.
But Baerbel Hoehn, regional agricultural minister in North Rhine-Westphalia state where the calf died last December on a farm in the town of Hoexter, said it was probably born in Germany after all.
"According to its papers and ear-markings there is no reason to doubt our original assumption," Hoehn said, dismissing suggestions that it might have been British-born as speculation.
German officials ordered on Wednesday the slaughter of over 5,000 British and Swiss cattle next week to calm consumer fears. Britain and Switzerland have recorded the largest number of BSE cases.
The officials also put the 14,000 calves of the British and Swiss cows under observation until tests established whether the Galloway calf was born in Germany to a British cow, as was first thought.
If experts determined that this was the case, it would add weight to fears that BSE can be maternally transferred and the 14,000 calves would definitely be destroyed.
An Agriculture Ministry spokesman said the 5,100 imported cattle would still be slaughtered, but not their 14,000 calves, if the calf proved to have been born outside Germany.
He said many documents relating to the calf from a farm in eastern Germany, where it was previously kept, were missing.
The Association of Cattle Breeders in the northern states of Schleswig-Holstein and Hamburg protested against the planned slaughter and vowed to take legal action to prevent it.
It said its members' cattle posed no danger to consumers and the 347 cattle imported from Britain to the two states were already under observation for any signs of BSE.
